title: Three layers of the past
title_target: Hade du varit i Göteborg förut?
goal: Tell a story in the past with three tenses — what happened, what has happened, and what had already happened before that.
bekal: choose between *flyttade* and *har flyttat* with confidence
form the pluperfect with *hade* + supine (*hade gått*, *hade läst*)
narrate a move or a journey step by step, in the right order
wave: Go back to Svenska 102, Unit 1 (Hur var helgen?): retell your last weekend aloud in five sentences, then add one sentence with *hade* that explains what you had done before it — *Jag var trött, för jag hade sovit dåligt.*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Första dagen på kontoret
dialogs.intro: A Monday at the end of August. Dian is starting a six-month internship (*praktik*) at a small design and IT company at Lindholmen, on the north bank of the river in Göteborg. Her new boss, Karin, meets her at reception.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Välkommen, Dian! Hittade du hit utan problem?
lines.id: Welcome, Dian! Did you find your way here all right?
lines.literal: welcome, Dian! found you here without problem?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Ja, jag tog färjan från Stenpiren. Det var första gången jag åkte båt till jobbet!
lines.id: Yes, I took the ferry from Stenpiren. It was the first time I'd ever gone to work by boat!
lines.literal: yes, I took ferry-the from Stenpiren. it was first time-the I went boat to job-the!

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Härligt. När kom du till Göteborg?
lines.id: Lovely. When did you arrive in Göteborg?
lines.literal: lovely. when came you to Göteborg?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: I torsdags. Jag har bott här i fyra dagar nu.
lines.id: Last Thursday. I've been living here for four days now.
lines.literal: in Thursday. I have lived here in four days now.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Och hur har det gått med boendet?
lines.id: And how have things gone with somewhere to live?
lines.literal: and how has it gone with living-the?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Bra, faktiskt. Jag hyr ett rum i andra hand i Majorna.
lines.id: Fine, actually. I'm subletting a room in Majorna.
lines.literal: well, actually. I rent a room in second hand in Majorna.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Vad bra. Det är inte lätt att hitta något här. Hade du varit i Göteborg förut?
lines.id: That's great. It isn't easy to find anything here. Had you been to Göteborg before?
lines.literal: what good. it is not easy to find something here. had you been in Göteborg before?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Bara en gång, för två år sedan. Min kompis Oskar hade bjudit hem mig till sina föräldrar.
lines.id: Just once, two years ago. My friend Oskar had invited me to his parents' place.
lines.literal: only one time, for two years since. my buddy Oskar had invited home me to his parents.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Då känner du redan staden lite. Har du träffat Mattias och Leila än?
lines.id: Then you already know the city a little. Have you met Mattias and Leila yet?
lines.literal: then know you already city-the little. have you met Mattias and Leila yet?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Nej, inte än. Jag har bara hälsat på killen i receptionen.
lines.id: No, not yet. I've only said hello to the guy at reception.
lines.literal: no, not yet. I have only greeted on guy-the in reception-the.

lines.speaker: Karin:
lines.text: Mattias har precis gått iväg på ett möte, men Leila sitter där borta. Kom, så presenterar jag dig.
lines.id: Mattias has just gone off to a meeting, but Leila is sitting over there. Come on, I'll introduce you.
lines.literal: Mattias has just gone away on a meeting, but Leila sits there away. come, so introduce I you.

notes: **Hittade du hit?** — Karin uses the simple past (*preteritum*) because she is asking about one finished event: the trip this morning. English does the same ("Did you find…?"). Note *hit* (to here), the direction word from Svenska 102: you find your way **hit**, but once you've arrived you are **här**.

**Jag har bott här i fyra dagar** — the perfect for something that began in the past and is still going on. English often says "I've **been living**"; Swedish has no -ing form and simply says *har bott*. Compare *Jag **bodde** i Stockholm i ett år* (I lived there for a year — it's over).

**I torsdags** (**ee TOOSH-dahks**) means "last Thursday". The *-s* ending on a day name always points backward: *i måndags*, *i lördags*. Without it, *på torsdag* points forward: "this coming Thursday".

**I andra hand** (**ee AHN-drah hahnd**), "second-hand", is how Sweden says "sublet". The main tenant, who has the *förstahandskontrakt*, rents the room or apartment out to you. Housing queues in big cities are years long, so most newcomers start out in a sublet, just like Dian.

**Hade du varit…?** — the pluperfect: *hade* + supine. It looks one step further back from a point that is already in the past, exactly like English "had been". Karin's question means: before you moved here last Thursday, had you ever been here?

**Färjan** (**FEHR-yahn**) — in Göteborg the river ferries (*Älvsnabben*) are part of ordinary public transport, so a bus or tram ticket works on the boat too. Notice *åka båt*, "go by boat", with no article — just like *åka buss* and *åka tåg*.

grammars.title: Preteritum or perfekt?
body: Swedish and English agree in most cases, so let English guide you — then look out for the few differences listed under the table. The deciding question is always the same: is the time **finished and named** (preteritum) or **open, unnamed, or still going** (perfekt)?

head: Situation
Tense
Example
rows: A finished time is named or obvious
A question about one specific finished event
Started in the past and still true
Jag **har bott** här i fyra dagar.
Mattias **har gått** iväg på ett möte.

after: **Difference 1:** English often uses the simple past with "just" or "already" ("He just left", "Did you eat already?"). Swedish needs the perfect: *Han **har precis gått***, ***Har** du redan **ätit**?*

**Difference 2:** English "I've been living / working / waiting" becomes a plain perfect: *jag har bott*, *jag har jobbat*, *jag har väntat*. For "how long", use *hur länge* + perfect: *Hur länge **har** du **bott** här?*

Once a story is under way, Swedes tell it in the preteritum, sentence after sentence — the perfect is for the frame ("I've moved to Göteborg"), the preteritum for the events ("I took the ferry, I met Karin…").

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Samtal med Elin
dialogs.intro: That evening Dian calls Elin in Stockholm from her new room in Majorna. Elin wants to hear everything.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Hej! Berätta nu – hur var första dagen?
lines.id: Hi! Come on, tell me — how was the first day?
lines.literal: hi! tell now – how was first day-the?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jättebra! Men morgonen började lite kaotiskt.
lines.id: Great! But the morning got off to a bit of a chaotic start.
lines.literal: giant-good! but morning-the began little chaotically.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Hur då?
lines.id: How so?
lines.literal: how then?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: När jag kom till hållplatsen hade spårvagnen redan gått.
lines.id: When I got to the stop, the tram had already left.
lines.literal: when I came to stop-the had tram-the already gone.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Typiskt! Vad gjorde du då?
lines.id: Typical! So what did you do?
lines.literal: typical! what did you then?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag tog en annan spårvagn till Stenpiren och sedan färjan över älven.
lines.id: I took another tram to Stenpiren and then the ferry across the river.
lines.literal: I took an other tram to Stenpiren and then ferry-the over river-the.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Smart! Hur visste du att det gick en färja?
lines.id: Smart! How did you know there was a ferry?
lines.literal: smart! how knew you that it went a ferry?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag hade läst om den på nätet kvällen innan.
lines.id: I'd read about it online the evening before.
lines.literal: I had read about it on net-the evening-the before.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Och kollegorna? Är de trevliga?
lines.id: And your colleagues? Are they nice?
lines.literal: and colleagues-the? are they nice?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Väldigt. Leila visade mig runt, och sedan fikade hela kontoret tillsammans.
lines.id: Very. Leila showed me around, and then the whole office had fika together.
lines.literal: very. Leila showed me around, and then fika-ed whole office-the together.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Har du hunnit packa upp allt?
lines.id: Have you had time to unpack everything?
lines.literal: have you had-time pack up all?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Nästan. Jag har packat upp kläderna, men böckerna står kvar i flyttkartongerna.
lines.id: Almost. I've unpacked my clothes, but the books are still in the moving boxes.
lines.literal: almost. I have packed up clothes-the, but books-the stand remaining in moving-boxes-the.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Ha ha, precis som när du flyttade till Södermalm!
lines.id: Ha ha, just like when you moved to Södermalm!
lines.literal: ha ha, exactly like when you moved to Södermalm!

notes: **När jag kom… hade spårvagnen redan gått** — the textbook pluperfect. There are two past events: Dian arriving and the tram leaving. The one that happened **first** gets *hade*. The little word *redan* (already) is a typical signal.
**Hur då?** — a very common follow-up: "How so? In what way?". Its cousins are *Varför då?* (Why's that?) and *Vem då?* (Who do you mean?). The *då* softens the question and shows you're interested.

**Kvällen innan** (**KVEL-len IN-nahn**) — "the evening before", counted from a point in the past. Compare *igår kväll*, "last night", counted from today. In storytelling you need the first kind: *dagen innan*, *veckan innan*, *dagen efter*, *året efter*.

**Fikade** — *fika* is both a noun (*en fika*) and a regular -ar verb (*fikar, fikade, har fikat*). Coffee and something sweet together with colleagues is a fixed part of the Swedish working day; Unit 18 is all about it.

**Har du hunnit…?** — *hunnit* is the supine of *hinna* (have time, make it). The perfect is natural here: Elin means "by now, so far". Remember the pattern: *hinna* + plain infinitive, no *att*: *hunnit packa upp*.

**Står kvar** — *kvar* (**kvahr**) means "still there, left over": *böckerna står kvar*, *det finns kaffe kvar*. Notice that the books **stand** in the boxes. Swedish likes positional verbs where English just says "are": books *står*, clothes *ligger*, a picture *sitter* or *hänger*.

grammars.title: The pluperfect: hade + supine
body: The pluperfect (*pluskvamperfekt*) is built exactly like the perfect, with *hade* instead of *har*. The supine is the same form you already know from Svenska 101 and 102 — it never changes.
after: Use it when you are already telling a story in the past and need to step one stage further back: *När jag kom hem **hade** Elin redan **lagat** mat.* (She cooked first, then I came.)
In a subordinate clause, BIFF puts *inte* before *hade*: *…eftersom jag **inte hade** ätit frukost.*

**A written shortcut:** in subordinate clauses Swedes often drop *har* and *hade* altogether, especially in writing: *Jag visste att spårvagnen redan (**hade**) gått.* *När jag (**har**) ätit, ringer jag.* You don't need to do it yourself, but you must recognize it — a lone supine in a subclause means a missing *har* or *hade*.

blocks.text: **Sedan** is almost always pronounced **sen** in speech, and many people write it that way too in messages. Keep the long form in anything formal, like the job application you'll write in Unit 20.

Every one of these words counts as one element at the start of a sentence, so the verb comes **next**, before the subject: ***Sedan tog** jag färjan.* ***Till slut hittade** jag kontoret.* This is the V2 rule from Svenska 101, and it is the single thing that most often goes wrong in learners' stories.

blocks.title: A story skeleton
items: **Frame (perfekt):** *Jag har flyttat till Göteborg.*
**Events (preteritum):** *I torsdags packade jag allt. Sedan tog jag tåget. På kvällen kom jag fram.*
**Background (pluperfekt):** *Oskar hade tipsat mig om rummet.*
**End (preteritum):** *Till slut somnade jag bland flyttkartongerna.*

blocks.text: Göteborg is Sweden's second city and the country's tram capital: its network is the largest in Scandinavia, and the local transport company is called *Västtrafik*. The city sits on the **Göta älv** river, which is why you often hear *på andra sidan älven* — "across the river" — the way Londoners talk about "south of the river". *Majorna*, where Dian lives, is an old working-class district by the harbor, now full of cafés and second-hand shops.
People from Göteborg are *göteborgare*, and they are famous across Sweden for being chatty, friendly and fond of puns — *göteborgsvitsar*. Oskar has warned Dian already.

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Svenska 102
items: Unit 1: say five things you did last week with time expressions — *i måndags*, *förra veckan*, *för tre dagar sedan*.
Unit 16: *i fyra dagar* (for, duration) vs *för fyra dagar sedan* (ago) vs *om fyra dagar* (in, future). Make one sentence with each.
Unit 2: make three time clauses with *innan* and *efter att* about your own last move, then push one event further back with *hade*: *Innan jag flyttade **hade** jag sålt min cykel.*
